Apple___Apple_scab.description: Apple scab is caused by the fungus Venturia inaequalis. It affects leaves, fruit, and twigs, leading to significant yield and aesthetic reduction in commercial orchards.
symptoms: Dull olive-green to brown velvety spots on the leaf upper surface.
Leaves can become distorted, curled, and drop prematurely.
Scabby, corky, dark lesions on mature fruits.
prevention: Select resistant apple cultivars (e.g., Liberty, Enterprise, Freedom).
Rake and dispose of fallen orchard leaves in autumn to disrupt fungal overwintering.
Prune canopies annually to improve air circulation and accelerate leaf drying.
management: Apply protective organically certified or approved copper/sulfur sprays early in spring.
Ensure proper row spacing to minimize prolonged leaf wetness periods.
Consult local extension officers for precise regional fungicide schedules.

Apple___Black_rot.description: Black rot is caused by the fungus Botryosphaeria obtusa. It affects apple leaves, bark cankers, and produces distinct 'frogeye' leaf spots and rotting fruit.
symptoms: Small purple flecks on leaves expanding into circular spots with tan centers ('frogeye' leaf spots).
Sunken reddish-brown cankers on branches and tree trunks.
Black, rotting, mummified fruits hanging on branches.
prevention: Prune out dead branches, twigs, and mummified fruits during the dormant season.
Avoid bark wounding during maintenance and pruning.
Maintain tree vigor through balanced fertility and drought mitigation.
management: Cut cankered wood at least 6-8 inches below visual symptom margins.
Burn or bury infected cuttings away from production blocks.
Apply labeled fungicides from silver tip stage through petal fall if infection pressure is high.

Apple___Cedar_apple_rust.description: Cedar apple rust is caused by the heteroecious fungus Gymnosporangium juniperi-virginianae, which requires both apple trees and Eastern red cedar (juniper) to complete its complex lifecycle.
symptoms: Bright yellow-orange or reddish spots on the upper leaf surface.
Small raised black dots (pycnia) appearing inside the orange spots.
Tube-like fungal structures (aecia) emerging from the underside of affected leaves.
prevention: Remove nearby Eastern red cedars or ornamental junipers within a 1-2 mile radius where feasible.
Plant rust-resistant apple cultivars.
Prune out galls from adjacent ornamental cedars before spring rains.
management: Apply preventative fungicides at the pink-bud stage through bloom when weather favors spore dispersal.
Monitor weather alerts for prolonged warm rain periods in early spring.

Apple___healthy.description: The apple foliage displays robust vigor, uniform green coloration, and an absence of fungal, bacterial, or necrotic pathogens.
symptoms: Clean, vibrant green leaves with smooth margins.
No visible chlorosis, necrosis, powdery growth, or rust pustules.
Vigorous shoot growth and normal petiole attachment.
prevention: Maintain consistent drip irrigation and regular soil nutrient testing.
Perform balanced seasonal dormant pruning.
management: Continue routine monitoring throughout the vegetative and fruiting phases.

Blueberry___healthy.description: Blueberry foliage exhibits healthy cell turgor, characteristic rich green leaves, and standard leaf cuticle structure without foliar pathogen indicators.
symptoms: Glossy green leaves free of blights, rusts, or leaf spots.
Uniform shoot elongation and healthy branch nodes.
prevention: Ensure acidic soil conditions (pH 4.5 to 5.2) with high organic matter.
Mulch root zones with pine bark or wood chips to conserve moisture.
management: Maintain balanced micro-irrigation and monitor for spotted wing drosophila and aphids.

Cherry_(including_sour)___Powdery_mildew.description: Powdery mildew on cherries is caused by Podosphaera clandestina. It infects young expanding leaves and shoots, reducing photosynthesis and fruit quality.
symptoms: White, powdery fungal mycelial patches on young leaves and stems.
Leaves curling upward, cupping, or blistering.
Stunted young vegetative terminal shoot growth.
prevention: Prune overcrowded canopies to permit maximum sunlight and dry breeze entry.
Avoid high-nitrogen fertilizers that stimulate excessive tender flushes.
Use drip irrigation rather than overhead sprinklers.
management: Apply agricultural horticultural oils or sulfur sprays at first detection.
Rotate fungicide modes of action (FRAC codes) to curb fungal resistance.

Cherry_(including_sour)___healthy.description: Cherry foliage is intact, structurally sound, and demonstrates normal photosynthetic activity free of foliar pathogens.
symptoms: Vibrant green leaves with crisp margins and intact venation.
Absence of fungal sporulation, powdery film, or shot-hole lesions.
prevention: Maintain orchard sanitary practices and timely winter spraying.
management: Observe standard seasonal orchard nutrition and IPM scouting.

Corn_(maize)___Cercospora_leaf_spot Gray.description: Gray leaf spot is caused by Cercospora zeae-maydis. It is a major foliar disease of maize favored by warm temperatures, high humidity, and prolonged morning dew.
symptoms: Small, pinpoint lesions with yellow halos on lower leaves.
Lesions elongate into rectangular, tan-to-gray spots bounded strictly by leaf veins.
Extensive blighting and premature leaf death in severe outbreaks.
prevention: Plant hybrid corn varieties with proven resistance traits.
Practice crop rotation with non-host crops like soybeans for at least 1-2 seasons.
Incorporate or bury crop residue where conservation tillage allows.
management: Scout fields around tasseling stage (VT to R1).
Apply labeled strobilurin or triazole fungicides if lesions appear on the ear leaf before blister stage.

Corn_(maize)___Common_rust_.description: Common rust is caused by the fungus Puccinia sorghi. It produces powdery pustules on both leaf surfaces and can cause chlorosis when severe.
symptoms: Small, circular to elongate reddish-brown or cinnamon-colored pustules (uredinia) scattered across both leaf surfaces.
Pustules rupture epidermal tissue, releasing powdery spores.
Yellow halos developing around dense clusters of pustules.
prevention: Select resistant hybrid corn cultivars with Rp single-gene or general resistance.
Plant early in the season to avoid peak airborne spore flights.
management: Foliar fungicides are typically required only on seed production fields or sensitive sweet corn when conditions remain cool and humid.

Corn_(maize)___Northern_Leaf_Blight.description: Northern Corn Leaf Blight (NCLB) is caused by Exserohilum turcicum. It creates elongated cigar-shaped lesions on maize foliage.
symptoms: Long, elliptical, cigar-shaped grayish-green to tan lesions (1 to 6 inches in length).
Dark olive sporulation visible within older lesions during damp periods.
Lesions coalesce, blighting entire leaves and accelerating lodging risk.
prevention: Use resistant hybrids containing Ht-resistance genes.
Rotate with non-cereal crops to lower overwintering inoculum in stubble.
Till and decompose corn stalks thoroughly after harvest.
management: Scout fields during silking. Apply targeted fungicides if lesions approach the ear leaf.

Corn_(maize)___healthy.description: Corn leaf blades show rich emerald coloration, strong parallel venation, and clear leaf tissue without fungal pustules or blights.
symptoms: Broad, intact green leaf blades without necrotic striping.
Absence of pustules, leaf spots, and chlorotic streaks.
prevention: Balanced soil nitrogen fertilization and adequate moisture management.
management: Routine field scouting across vegetative and reproductive growth stages.

Grape___Black_rot.description: Black rot is caused by Guignardia bidwellii. It attacks all green tissues of grapevine, especially developing fruit clusters and young leaves.
symptoms: Circular reddish-brown leaf spots with distinct dark brown margins.
Tiny black specks (pycnidia) arranged in rings inside the leaf spots.
Infected berries shrivel, blacken, and turn into hard, mummified raisins.
prevention: Remove and destroy all mummified berries from the vine and trellis ground during winter pruning.
Maintain open vine canopies through shoot thinning and leaf pulling.
management: Apply preventative fungicide treatments starting at 1-inch shoot growth through post-bloom.
Promptly prune symptomatic shoots to arrest secondary spread.

Grape___Esca_(Black_Measles).description: Esca is a complex trunk disease caused by a succession of fungal pathogens (including Phaeomoniella chlamydospora and Phaeoacremonium minimum).
symptoms: 'Tiger-stripe' chlorotic and necrotic patterns between leaf veins.
Spots on berries (black measles) resembling dark purple speckles.
Severe 'apoplexy' leading to sudden wilt and collapse of entire vines during hot spells.
prevention: Protect winter pruning wounds with wound sealants or biocontrol agents.
Avoid pruning during wet periods when fungal spores are airborne.
Purchase certified clean vine stock from reputable nurseries.
management: Perform remedial surgery (trunk renewal) by cutting below necrotic vascular wood.
Uproot and destroy critically devastated vines.

Grape___Leaf_blight_(Isariopsis_Leaf_Spo.description: Leaf blight in grapevines is caused by Phaeoisariopsis vitis (Isariopsis clavispora), causing late-season premature defoliation in warm, humid regions.
symptoms: Irregular brown or black lesions on the upper leaf surface.
Lesions surrounded by diffuse yellow halo margins.
Velvety gray or dark brown spore mass on the lower surface of lesions.
prevention: Ensure proper vineyard canopy training to facilitate air movement.
Clear fallen grapevine leaves after harvest.
management: Apply preventative copper-based sprays or broad-spectrum protectants following fruit harvest if conditions stay moist.

Grape___healthy.description: Grapevine leaves display uniform palmate lobes, deep green color, intact margins, and clean petiole connections.
symptoms: Smooth, clean foliage with uniform green pigmentation.
No spotting, tiger-striping, powdery patches, or berry rot.
prevention: Optimal trellis management, canopy hedging, and integrated pest scouting.
management: Continue standard seasonal vineyard spray schedules and water management.

Orange___Haunglongbing_(Citrus_greening).description: Huanglongbing (HLB) is a destructive bacterial disease caused by Candidatus Liberibacter asiaticus, transmitted primarily by the Asian citrus psyllid (Diaphorina citri).
symptoms: Asymmetric blotchy mottling of leaf blades across vein boundaries.
Yellowing of veins followed by leaf drop and twig dieback.
Small, lopsided, poorly colored fruit with bitter taste and aborted seeds.
prevention: Strict vector control targeting Asian citrus psyllid populations using IPM protocols.
Plant only certified disease-free citrus trees produced under insect-proof screenhouses.
Quarantine and avoid transporting citrus plant material across restricted regions.
management: Remove infected trees promptly to eliminate infection sources for neighboring blocks.
Provide supplemental foliar micronutrients to support tree health temporarily.

Peach___Bacterial_spot.description: Bacterial spot is caused by Xanthomonas arboricola pv. pruni, attacking leaves, twigs, and stone fruits in sandy soils and humid, windy climates.
symptoms: Water-soaked polygonal angular spots on leaves.
Lesion centers dry out and drop out, creating a 'shot-hole' appearance.
Pitted, cracked, gummy lesions on peach fruits.
prevention: Plant less susceptible cultivars adapted to regional microclimates.
Avoid planting in highly windswept locations without suitable windbreaks.
Prevent excessive nitrogen applications that encourage late succulent flushes.
management: Apply protective dormant copper sprays before bud swell.
Use oxytetracycline sprays where permitted during active risk periods.

Peach___healthy.description: Peach foliage is elongated, lanceolate, supple, and shows normal chlorophyll density with no shot-holes or bacterial spots.
symptoms: Clean lanceolate leaves with smooth serrated margins.
Free of shot-hole perforations, leaf curling, or cankers.
prevention: Standard dormant stone-fruit hygiene and balanced fertilization.
management: Routine orchard scouting and drip irrigation scheduling.

Pepper,_bell___Bacterial_spot.description: Bacterial spot on bell pepper is caused by Xanthomonas euvesicatoria and related species. It thrives during warm rainy periods.
symptoms: Small circular or irregular water-soaked spots on leaves.
Spots darken to brown with dark borders and may have light tan centers.
Severe yellowing and premature leaf shedding, exposing fruit to sunscald.
prevention: Use certified disease-free, hot-water-treated seed.
Choose resistant bell pepper varieties (Xanthomonas races 1-10 resistance).
Sanitize greenhouse trays, flats, and pruning tools regularly.
management: Avoid overhead sprinkler irrigation and working in wet fields.
Apply preventative copper-mancozeb tank mixes as recommended by university extension.

Pepper,_bell___healthy.description: Bell pepper leaves are lustrous, dark green, ovate, and show clear healthy leaf venation.
symptoms: Glossy green leaves with uniform coloration.
Absence of water-soaked spots, necrotic rims, or curling.
prevention: Maintain consistent soil moisture and avoid nitrogen imbalance.
management: Perform periodic scouting for thrips, mites, and aphids.

Potato___Early_blight.description: Early blight is caused by the fungal pathogen Alternaria solani. It primarily damages older foliage and can cause defoliation and tuber quality loss.
symptoms: Dark brown to black spots developing concentric rings ('target-board' or bullseye pattern).
Spots typically originate on older, lower canopy leaves first.
Yellow chlorotic halos surrounding expanding lesions.
prevention: Rotate potatoes with non-solanaceous crops on a 3-year minimum cycle.
Maintain adequate plant nitrogen and potassium nutrition to avoid early senescence.
Ensure proper hill spacing to promote rapid canopy drying.
management: Apply protectant fungicides (chlorothalonil, mancozeb) according to blight forecast models.
Eliminate cull piles and volunteer potato plants.

Potato___Late_blight.description: Late blight is caused by the oomycete Phytophthora infestans. It is an aggressive, historically destructive foliar and tuber disease favored by cool, wet conditions.
symptoms: Water-soaked, pale to dark green lesions turning rapidly brown or purplish-black.
White fuzzy mildew growth on the undersides of lesions during humid or dewy mornings.
Rapidly wilting and collapsing foliage emitting a distinct decaying odor.
prevention: Plant exclusively certified pathogen-free seed tubers.
Eliminate all cull piles, volunteer potatoes, and nightshade weeds.
Consult regional disease warning alerts (e.g., BlightCast).
management: Immediately apply targeted anti-oomycete protectant or translaminar fungicides upon local outbreak warning.
Destroy heavily blighted foliage prior to tuber harvest to prevent spore wash into soil.

Potato___healthy.description: Potato foliage shows vigorous compound leaves, rich chlorophyll pigmentation, and crisp margins without foliar blights.
symptoms: Vibrant green compound leaflets without necrosis.
Absence of concentric ring lesions or water-soaked patches.
prevention: Proper hilling, balanced fertility, and clean seed tuber sourcing.
management: Continue standard preventive fungicide forecasting and pest monitoring.

Raspberry___healthy.description: Raspberry canes and leaves display vigorous vegetative growth, normal trifoliate leaf development, and healthy green tissue.
symptoms: Bright green serrated leaflets with pale undersides.
Absence of cane blight, rust pustules, or viral mosaic mottling.
prevention: Select certified virus-indexed cane stock.
Prune floricanes immediately after fruiting to promote primocane airflow.
management: Maintain drip irrigation and mulch beds with clean straw or wood chips.

Soybean___healthy.description: Soybean foliage exhibits healthy trifoliate leaves, robust nodulation support, and no signs of bacterial or fungal leaf scorch.
symptoms: Uniform green trifoliate leaflets.
No rust pustules, frogeye leaf spots, or sudden death syndrome chlorosis.
prevention: Practice crop rotation with maize and use certified inoculated seed.
management: Scout for soybean cyst nematodes and foliar pests during canopy closure.

Squash___Powdery_mildew.description: Powdery mildew on cucurbits is caused by Podosphaera xanthii. It affects both leaf surfaces and stems, accelerating vine decline and fruit sunburn.
symptoms: White powdery fungal spots developing on crowns, stems, and both leaf surfaces.
Foliage turning yellow, then brown, brittle, and papery.
Premature leaf drop leading to exposed fruits and reduced fruit sweetness.
prevention: Select resistant or tolerant squash and pumpkin cultivars.
Plant in full sun with adequate row and plant spacing.
Avoid excess nitrogen feeding that produces excessive succulent vine growth.
management: Apply potassium bicarbonate, neem oil, or horticultural oils at early sign.
Use systemic fungicides rotated by FRAC groups if disease pressure escalates.

Strawberry___Leaf_scorch.description: Leaf scorch is caused by the fungus Diplocarpon earlianum. It infects strawberry foliage, calyxes, and stolons, reducing plant vigor.
symptoms: Numerous irregular purplish spots on upper leaf surfaces without clear white centers.
Lesions enlarge and merge, causing leaf margins to curl upward and turn brown/scorched.
In severe cases, entire leaflets appear burned and desiccated.
prevention: Select certified disease-free strawberry plugs or runners.
Avoid excessive overhead sprinkling; water early in the morning.
Renovate strawberry beds after harvest by mowing and removing dead leaves.
management: Apply preventative biofungicides or copper sprays at initial vegetative flush.
Remove heavily infected plants to limit secondary conidial transmission.

Strawberry___healthy.description: Strawberry plant foliage shows typical serrated trifoliate leaves with vibrant green coloration and sturdy petioles.
symptoms: Clean, deep green trifoliate leaves.
Absence of purple scorch lesions, powdery mildew, or leaf spot halving.
prevention: Plant in well-drained raised beds with plastic mulch or straw.
management: Maintain adequate moisture and replenish seasonal mulch.

Tomato___Bacterial_spot.description: Bacterial spot in tomato is caused by several species of Xanthomonas (X. vesicatoria, X. euvesicatoria, X. perforans, X. gardneri). It thrives in warm, wet climates.
symptoms: Small, dark, greasy or water-soaked circular lesions on foliage.
Lesions turn necrotic, brown-black, and may have a faint yellow halo.
Severe defoliation starting from lower foliage upward.
prevention: Plant certified pathogen-tested seeds or hot-water-treated seeds.
Sanitize stakes, cages, and greenhouse benches between seasons.
Avoid handling plants or cultivating when foliage is wet from dew or rain.
management: Apply copper bactericides combined with mancozeb to overcome copper tolerance.
Utilize bacteriophage treatments where available as biological alternatives.

Tomato___Early_blight.description: Early blight is caused by the necrotrophic fungus Alternaria linariae (formerly Alternaria solani). It commonly affects field and greenhouse tomatoes.
symptoms: Circular brown or black spots with distinct concentric rings ('target-like' pattern).
Surrounding leaf tissue becomes chlorotic (yellow) as toxins spread.
Lower leaves wither and fall, progressing upward along the stem.
prevention: Mulch soil around plants to prevent soilborne fungal spores from splashing up.
Prune bottom suckers and lower foliage up to 12 inches to maintain dry airflow.
Rotate with non-solanaceous crops on a 2-3 year cycle.
management: Apply copper, chlorothalonil, or bio-fungicide sprays at the first indication of lower leaf spotting.
Remove and compost or dispose of infected lower leaves.

Tomato___Late_blight.description: Late blight is caused by the destructive oomycete Phytophthora infestans. Under cool and moist weather, it can rapidly destroy entire tomato plots.
symptoms: Large, irregularly shaped, water-soaked oily grayish-green lesions on leaves and stems.
Lesions rapidly expand, turning dark brown, purplish, or black.
Delicate white fungal-like downy growth on leaf undersides in humid conditions.
prevention: Select resistant tomato cultivars (e.g., Mountain Magic, Defiant, Iron Lady).
Space plants generously to promote rapid canopy drying.
Avoid planting tomatoes adjacent to potatoes.
management: Apply protective anti-oomycete fungicides immediately upon regional alert.
Bag and remove blighted plants immediately; do not compost infected tissue.

Tomato___Leaf_Mold.description: Tomato leaf mold is caused by Passalora fulva (formerly Cladosporium fulvum). It is a major issue in high tunnels and greenhouses with high relative humidity.
symptoms: Pale green to pale yellow chlorotic spots with indefinite margins on upper leaf surfaces.
Dense, olive-green to grayish-brown velvety fungal mold on leaf undersides.
Leaves turn yellow, curl, and die prematurely.
prevention: Improve greenhouse ventilation and lower relative humidity below 85%.
Use circulating horizontal airflow fans.
Grow leaf-mold resistant tomato hybrids (carrying Cf resistance genes).
management: Apply approved preventative biofungicides (Bacillus subtilis) or copper formulations.
Prune lower suckers to improve light penetration and air movement.

Tomato___Septoria_leaf_spot.description: Septoria leaf spot is caused by Septoria lycopersici. It causes severe defoliation during prolonged warm, wet weather.
symptoms: Small, numerous circular spots with dark brown margins and grayish-white centers.
Tiny black specks (pycnidia) clearly visible in the center of mature spots.
Leaves turn yellow and drop prematurely, starting from the base of the vine.
prevention: Apply mulch to prevent splash dissemination of spores from the ground.
Avoid overhead watering; use soaker hoses or drip lines.
Eradicate solanaceous weeds such as horse nettle and nightshade around fields.
management: Pick off and destroy infected lower leaves early in the season.
Apply protectant fungicides (chlorothalonil or copper) on a preventative schedule.

Tomato___Spider_mites Two-spotted_spider.description: Damage caused by Tetranychus urticae. Mites puncture plant cells on the leaf underside to suck sap, thriving in hot, dry, dusty conditions.
symptoms: Fine yellow or white stippling (pinpoint speckles) on the upper leaf surface.
Fine silk webbing on leaf undersides and shoot tips.
Leaves turn bronze, dry out, and drop prematurely in heavy infestations.
prevention: Keep walkways wet or covered to reduce dust that suppresses natural mite predators.
Avoid broad-spectrum synthetic pyrethroids that eliminate predatory mites.
Conserve or release predatory mites (e.g., Phytoseiulus persimilis).
management: Wash plant foliage with strong water sprays to dislodge mites and webs.
Apply insecticidal soaps or horticultural oils directly to leaf undersides.

Tomato___Target_Spot.description: Target spot is caused by the fungus Corynespora cassiicola. It affects leaves, stems, and fruit under warm, humid conditions.
symptoms: Small pinpoint brown spots on leaves expanding into circular brown lesions.
Lesions feature subtle concentric rings with light brown centers.
Pitted sunken dark lesions on green or ripe tomato fruit.
prevention: Ensure wide plant spacing and prune suckers to optimize air circulation.
Avoid working in tomato beds while morning dew is present.
Rotate fields away from solanaceous and cucurbit crops.
management: Apply preventative fungicides with active ingredients from FRAC group 7 or 11.
Scout lower canopies regularly for early lesion identification.

Tomato___Tomato_Yellow_Leaf_Curl_Virus.description: TYLCV is a destructive begomovirus transmitted by the sweetpotato whitefly (Bemisia tabaci). It causes severe stunting and catastrophic fruit loss.
symptoms: Leaves become distinctly cupped, curled upward, and reduced in size.
Pronounced interveinal chlorosis and yellow margins on young leaves.
Severe plant stunting with bushy, upright growth and massive flower drop.
prevention: Grow TYLCV-resistant or tolerant cultivars (e.g., Tygress, Skyway, Charger).
Install fine insect mesh (50-mesh screen) in nursery and greenhouse structures.
Use yellow sticky traps to monitor and trap whitefly vectors.
management: Apply insecticidal soaps, horticultural oils, or systemic insecticides to manage whiteflies.
Immediately rogue out and destroy virus-infected plants in plastic bags.

Tomato___Tomato_mosaic_virus.description: Tomato mosaic virus is a highly stable tobamovirus easily transmitted mechanically through pruning, handling, grafting, and contaminated tools.
symptoms: Mottling with alternating light and dark green patches on leaves.
Distorted, blistered, or strap-like 'shoestring' leaves.
Internal browning (brown wall) of tomato fruits.
prevention: Grow ToMV-resistant cultivars (marked with 'T' or 'ToMV' code).
Wash hands with soap or 20% nonfat dry milk solution before handling plants.
Disinfect all pruning shears with a 10% household bleach solution between plants.
management: Immediately isolate and discard infected plants; there is no chemical cure for viral infections.
Avoid tobacco use near tomato plants, as tobacco products can harbor tobamoviruses.

Tomato___healthy.description: Tomato plant exhibits strong indeterminate/determinate vigor, uniform green compound leaves, robust trichomes, and clear petiole junctions.
symptoms: Rich green compound leaves with crisp margins and healthy glandular hairs.
Absence of chlorosis, target spots, mold, curling, or necrosis.
prevention: Proper staking, drip irrigation, balanced nitrogen/calcium nutrition, and mulching.
management: Continue routine crop scouting and integrated pest management (IPM).
